paper.title: Low-density nano-bainitic Al–C steels
paper.journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
paper.research_type: mixed (predominantly experimental with MatCalc computational/simulation support)
paper.paper_scope: Systematic study of bainitic transformation kinetics and tensile properties (UTS, elongation, hardness) of five low-density nano-bainitic high C–Al steels (S1–S5; 0.60–1.10 wt.% C, 3.92–8.08 wt.% Al, with Ti/Ni/B/Mo/Si variations) under different austenitizing (1150/1220/1250 °C) and austempering (270–365 °C) conditions, supported by LOM/SEM/EDX/EBSD/XRD and MatCalc simulations.

alloys.description: Boron-microalloyed high C–Al low-density nano-bainitic steel designed to minimize density and bainitic transformation time; ~6 wt.% Al with high C for full austenitization.
alloys.alloys_notes: Mn limited to ~1 wt.% to stabilize ferrite and accelerate transformation; Si kept low at ~0.3 wt.% since Al also suppresses carbide precipitation; Mo and B added for hardenability. No Ni or Ti reported.

source.reason: Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt.%) of steel grade S1, and Section 2.1 (Alloy design) describes the design rationale (Al 5.8–8 wt.%, Mn ≤1 wt.%, high C 0.9–1.0 wt.%, low Si 0.3 wt.%, Mo for hardenability, B microalloying).

alloys.description: Boron-microalloyed high C–Al low-density nano-bainitic steel closely related to S1 but with slightly higher C (~1.10 wt.%).
alloys.alloys_notes: Differs from S1 mainly by ~0.1 wt.% higher C content; no Ni or Ti reported.

source.reason: Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt.%) of steel grade S2; Section 2.1 describes the high C–Al design group (S1–S4).

alloys.description: Highest-Al low-density nano-bainitic steel (~8.08 wt.% Al) that retains polygonal ferrite even at elevated austenitizing temperatures; slowest bainitic transformation.
alloys.alloys_notes: Very high Al content (~8 wt.%) stabilizes ferrite; residual polygonal ferrite (~8.2 % at 1220 °C) could not be fully eliminated within the practical window. No Ni or Ti reported.

source.reason: Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt.%) of steel grade S3; Section 2.1 and Section 3.1 discuss its very high Al content and ferrite retention.

alloys.description: Ti-microalloyed low-density nano-bainitic steel with slightly lower Al and C than S1–S3 plus 0.78 wt.% Ni; Ti addition promotes TiMoC precipitation for refined microstructure and improved strength–ductility balance.
alloys.alloys_notes: Slightly lower Al to suppress polygonal ferrite; reduced C to accelerate transformation and mitigate brittleness; 0.78 % Ni added to prevent polygonal ferrite formation; Ti microalloying applied to enhance bainitic transformation (forms TiMoC).

source.reason: Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt.%) of steel grade S4; Section 2.1 describes the lower Al/C design and Ti microalloying plus 0.78 % Ni.

alloys.description: Lower-alloying-concept low-density nano-bainitic steel with 0.60 wt.% C and 3.92 wt.% Al plus 0.78 wt.% Ni; fastest bainitic transformation kinetics.
alloys.alloys_notes: No B or Ti reported; Ni (0.78 %) minimized due to cost and austenite-stabilization effect, added to promote αp-free microstructure.

source.reason: Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt.%) of steel grade S5; Section 2.1 describes the lower alloying concept (0.6 % C, 3.92 % Al, 0.78 % Ni).

processes.processes_notes: Shared heat-treatment schedule applied to S1, S2 and S4. All steels were first homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h in argon and step-by-step hot rolled to ~11 mm before heat treatment.

unmapped_findings: MatCalc TTP simulations show primary (Fe,M)xCy carbides precipitate during cooling/austenitizing (700–1150 °C in S1 and S3, 700–1000 °C in S5) rather than during austempering, and in S4 initial nucleation at 700–950 °C is subsequently suppressed by the counter-coarsening effect of the Ti–Mo–C system.

Ti-microalloying in S4 forms stable TiMoC complex precipitates that suppress deleterious (Fe,M)xCy, MoC and possibly κ-carbide phases, refine the microstructure, and promote bainite nucleation but eventually slow transformation via bainitic sheaf impingement.

Bainitic ferrite lamellar thickness Lt(t) ranges ~34–41 nm at low austempering temperature and ~55–68 nm at higher temperature across the studied steels; S4 thickness (56–58 nm) is nearly independent of austenitizing temperature.
The paper reports no B or Ti addition for S5 and no Ni/Ti for S1–S3; B (0.0026–0.0039 wt.%) is present only in S1–S4.
